adversarial_test_results.prompt: The development of the electron microscope began in the 1920s, when physicists realized that the resolving power of any optical instrument is limited by the wavelength of the illumination it uses. Because electrons have a wavelength thousands of times shorter than visible light, a beam of electrons could in principle reveal structures far below the diffraction limit that constrained the best optical microscopes. In 1931, Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll, working at the Technical University of Berlin, assembled the first instrument that used magnetic lenses to focus an electron beam, and within a few years the device had been refined into a practical tool for biology and materials science. The early microscopes operated by transmitting electrons through specimens thinner than a few hundred nanometres, and the contrast in the resulting images depended on how strongly different regions of the specimen scattered the beam. Investigators soon learned that heavy-metal stains such as osmium tetroxide could be used to enhance that contrast, and the technique became a cornerstone of cell biology. Subsequent improvements followed two distinct paths. The first was the development of the scanning electron microscope, which rastered a finely focused probe across the surface of a specimen and collected secondary electrons emitted from each point; this produced images of surface topography with a striking three-dimensional appearance. The second was the introduction of aberration correction, in which multipole lenses compensate for the spherical and chromatic defects that had long limited resolution. By the 1980s, instruments equipped with field-emission sources and computer-controlled lens currents could resolve individual atoms in crystalline specimens, and the technique had spread from physics departments into chemistry, geology and medicine. Commercial manufacturers in Japan, Germany and the United States competed to produce ever more stable columns, and the price of a top-of-the-line instrument rose accordingly. Detectors improved as well, from photographic plates to direct electron cameras that record images at high frame rates and let the motion of beam-sensitive samples be corrected computationally. Modern laboratories now rely on cryogenic sample preparation, in which specimens are vitrified in liquid ethane rather than chemically fixed, so that delicate protein assemblies are preserved in a state close to their native conformation. The decisive contribution, however, remained the original insight that a beam of electrons can be focused by magnetic fields in much the same way that glass focuses light, an idea whose practical realization was recognized when Ernst Ruska shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986.
